Node.js runtime spawning OS command interpreter (joyfill RAT ss_eval) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts node.exe/npm spawning a shell or scripting interpreter (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, /bin/sh, /bin/bash, wscript, cscript). The joyfill RAT exposes an ss_eval arbitrary-code verb over Socket.IO; command execution from a Node runtime on a developer box is the RAT acting on objectives. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #3 grounded in the article's stated ss_eval arbitrary-code-execution verb; node→interpreter is unusual outside build tooling and the parent constraint on node.exe/npm keeps it campaign-relevant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm lifecycle scripts (node spawning cmd.exe to run pre/post hooks)
  • node-gyp / native module builds shelling to cmd/sh
  • cross-env or shx wrappers invoking a shell
  • husky git hooks running through node then sh
  • CI pipelines where node orchestrates shell steps
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","husky","cross-env","npm run","lifecycle"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line for recon/download/exfil content; benign npm hooks are short and repo-scoped. 2) Contain: if the shell content is suspicious, isolate host and kill the node tree. 3) Hunt: check the same host for @joyfill package presence, C2 IP contact, and the python.exe stealer spawn.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","sh","bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "npm.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","\\sh","\\bash")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js runtime spawning host reconnaissance utilities (joyfill RAT ss_info) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts node.exe/npm spawning system-discovery tools (whoami, systeminfo, ipconfig, netstat, wmic, hostname, tasklist, net.exe). The joyfill RAT's ss_info verb collects host information; discovery utilities launched from a Node runtime on a developer workstation indicate RAT enumeration prior to exfiltration. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #4, anchored to the RAT's documented ss_info verb; the 2+-distinct-tool burst threshold separates malware enumeration from an occasional legit ipconfig call inside a node script. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised
ATT&CKT1033 T1082 T1016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node dev-tooling that calls ipconfig/hostname for local network config (e.g. dev-server host detection)
  • Diagnostics/telemetry scripts in an Electron app gathering system info
  • CI health-check scripts running systeminfo/netstat
  • A developer's own troubleshooting via a node REPL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("healthcheck","diagnostics","dev-server")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node parent is not a known diagnostics tool; a burst of whoami+systeminfo+ipconfig within minutes is RAT enumeration. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill node tree, capture @joyfill package artifacts. 3) Hunt: pivot to credential-access (python.exe stealer), C2 IP egress, and persistence file writes on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe","wmic.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","net.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(FileName), Tools = make_set(FileName), any(ProcessCommandLine)
          by bin(Timestamp, 10m), DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctTools >= 2   // 2+ distinct recon tools from node within 10m = enumeration burst
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "npm.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe","wmic.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","net.exe")
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(NewProcessName), Tools = make_set(NewProcessName)
          by bin(TimeGenerated, 10m), Computer, Account
| where DistinctTools >= 2
| order by TimeGenerated desc

joyfill RAT persistence: self-reload injected into VS Code/Discord/GitHub Desktop/npm CLI AIInstallation High
Hunts a node.exe process modifying the developer-tool files the joyfill RAT injects its self-reloading block into: the @vscode/deviceid module (VS Code/Cursor/Antigravity), Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI. Node writing to these specific IDE/tool JS files is a high-fidelity persistence signal. Rationale: Uses the exact persistence targets named in the article and corroborated by JFrog (@vscode/deviceid, Discord desktop core, GitHub Desktop main.js, global npm CLI). Node writing to another tool's shipped JS is rare and high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise
ATT&CKT1554 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate VS Code / Cursor / GitHub Desktop auto-updater rewriting its own bundled files
  • npm self-update rewriting npm-cli.js during `npm install -g npm`
  • Discord client auto-update replacing core module
  • Reinstall/repair of these apps via their own installers (which use their own binaries, not node.exe)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","update") == false or FolderPath has "deviceid"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writer is node.exe/npm rather than the app's own updater; diff the modified file for an appended obfuscated self-reload block (look for the 9-0135-3 marker or a global['!'] assignment). 2) Contain: isolate host, restore clean copies of the tampered files, kill node processes. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same file writes and for @joyfill 2773 beta package installs.

| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\@vscode\deviceid", @"\GitHub Desktop\", @"\npm\bin", @"\node_modules\npm\lib")
     or (FolderPath has "discord" and FileName endswith ".js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\@vscode\deviceid", @"\GitHub Desktop\", @"\npm\bin", @"\node_modules\npm\lib")
     or (TargetFilePath has "discord" and TargetFileName endswith ".js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

joyfill RAT credential stealer: python spawned by Node.js runtime AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a node.exe/npm process spawning python (python.exe, python3, pythonw.exe) — the joyfill RAT stages a Python infostealer that harvests browser data, extension wallets/password managers, Git and GitHub CLI credentials, and OS keychains. A Python child of a Node runtime on a developer box is anomalous and maps directly to the stealer stage. Rationale: The article states the RAT 'stages a Python infostealer'; node→python is a rare parent/child pair in normal JS development and cleanly encodes the credential-theft stage without generic browser-file-access noise. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node projects with native/Python build steps (node-gyp invoking python for gyp)
  • ML/data tooling where a node CLI orchestrates python scripts
  • Cross-language monorepos where node task runners call python
  • Electron apps bundling a python helper
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has_any ("gyp","binding.gyp","node-gyp","configure.py")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the python child command line and script path — gyp/build invocations reference binding.gyp; a stealer reads browser/keychain paths. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process tree, and immediately rotate browser-stored, Git, GitHub CLI, and keychain credentials for the user. 3) Hunt: look for the encrypted-archive upload to the C2 IPs and the on-chain resolution traffic on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python","pythonw.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "npm.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3","pythonw.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: joyfill RAT python credential stealer spawn
id: f0d3a915-7c26-4e8b-9d14-2a6f8b0c1e77
description: node.exe or npm spawning python, matching the joyfill RAT staged Python infostealer
references:

  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1059.006

  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\npm.exe) @Image:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\python3)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(node\.exe|npm\.exe)/i ImageFileName=/(python3?|pythonw)(\.exe)?$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","node","npm.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("python.exe","python3","python","pythonw.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","node","npm.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("python.exe","python3","python","pythonw.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Compromised @joyfill 2773-beta package artifacts on disk (hash/path match) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts on-disk presence of the trojanised @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts 2773 beta bundles, by the two published malicious SHA-256 hashes and by node_modules path. Surfaces workstations, CI runners, and build images that pulled the compromised packages so they can be remediated and credentials rotated. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #2 using the two exact malicious SHA-256 hashes from the IOC block plus the scoped @joyfill node_modules path, giving a deterministic disk-presence detection across dev boxes, CI runners, and build images. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally holding the sample for analysis
  • Malware sandbox/detonation host with the packages staged
  • Internal registry mirror that cached the bad versions before quarantine (still a true finding to remediate)
  • Legitimate @joyfill install of a non-2773 clean version matching only on path, not hash — path clause surfaces all @joyfill, so validate version
Suppression filter
| where SHA256 in ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18","36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or FileName in~ ("package.json")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is a real 2773-beta version (check the package.json version under the @joyfill folder) vs a clean pinned release. 2) Contain: remove the version from lockfiles, caches, internal mirrors, and build images; pin to a known-good release published before 2026-07-28. 3) Hunt: on every host with a hit, rotate credentials and search for C2 IP egress, the node -e second stage, and dev-tool persistence writes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18","36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
     or FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\@joyfill\components", @"\node_modules\@joyfill\layouts")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18","36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
     or TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\@joyfill\components", @"\node_modules\@joyfill\layouts")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Compromised @joyfill 2773-beta package on disk

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse (< 2.0.2, CVE-2026-54658) in software inventory AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts/containers running @hypequery/clickhouse below the patched 2.0.2 release that carries the escapeValue() SQL-injection flaw (CVE-2026-54658). This is exposure hunting for the specific vulnerable npm package named in the advisory, not a behavioural attack detection. Rationale: Direct match on the CVE id from the advisory (CVE-2026-54658) plus the affected package @hypequery/clickhouse < 2.0.2; MDVM/CIM Vulnerabilities inventory is the cleanest place to enumerate exposed assets before exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package present in a dev/test container that is not internet-exposed and takes no user-controlled parameters
  • App wraps hypequery only with server-generated (non-user) parameter values, so the flaw is not reachable
  • Vendored copy pinned at 2.0.2+ but TVM fingerprint lags and still shows old metadata
  • Internal tooling image flagged but decommissioned / not running
  • Package inventoried as a transitive dependency that is never invoked at runtime
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is truly < 2.0.2 and whether the host serves user-controlled ClickHouse queries (internet-facing API vs internal batch job). 2) Contain: prioritise upgrade to @hypequery/clickhouse 2.0.2 on any asset that passes untrusted input as query parameters; where patching lags, front the endpoint with a WAF rule blocking backslash-terminated parameter values. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 to check whether the exposed asset has already received backslash-quote injection payloads in web or ClickHouse query logs.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-54658"
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-54658"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-54658" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-54658" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
ClickHouse SQLi via trailing backslash quote-escape in web/API parameters (CVE-2026-54658) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests whose parameter values carry the CVE-2026-54658 exploitation signature — a backslash immediately before a single quote (raw \' or URL-encoded %5c%27) used to break out of the escapeValue() string literal — combined with SQL syntax tokens. Targets the actual exploitation attempt against apps using @hypequery/clickhouse. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE-2026-54658 breakout mechanic from the advisory (trailing backslash escaping the closing single quote in escapeValue()) rendered as raw \' and URL-encoded %5c%27, gated by SQL tokens so it is specific to injection rather than any backslash in a URL. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows file paths in a legitimate parameter (e.g. ?path=C:\dir\) that happen to precede a quote plus a word like 'select'
  • Security scanners / DAST (Burp, sqlmap, Acunetix) probing the app in an authorized test
  • Rich-text or code-snippet form fields legitimately containing backslashes and SQL keywords
  • Analytics dashboards passing SQL fragments as URL parameters by design
  • WAF-normalised double-encoding producing %255c%2527 that this rule under-matches (tune encoding variants)
Suppression filter
| where not (csUriQuery matches regex @"(?i)[a-z]:%5c" and csUserAgent has_any ("sqlmap","nuclei","acunetix","burp"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode csUriQuery and confirm a backslash actually terminates a parameter value before a quote followed by injected SQL; check src IP reputation and whether the target app depends on @hypequery/clickhouse. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and add a rule rejecting parameter values ending in backslash to ClickHouse-backed endpoints; if the app is < 2.0.2, expedite the patch. 3) Hunt: correlate the same src/time to UC3 (ClickHouse query log) to confirm whether the injection reached the database, and review responses/status codes for data exfiltration volume.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
// backslash-quote escape (raw or URL-encoded) = the CVE-2026-54658 breakout primitive
| where csUriQuery matches regex @"(?i)(%5c%27|%5c'|\\')"
// require SQL syntax alongside the escape to cut generic noise
| where csUriQuery has_any ("union","select","information_schema","sleep(","benchmark(","concat(")
    or csUriQuery contains "--" or csUriQuery contains "/*"
    or csUriQuery matches regex @"(?i)or[%20\s]+\d+=\d+"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs WebDAV --no-delete bypass: DELETE blocked (403) then MOVE succeeds (2xx) on same path AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core CVE-2026-64863 exploit signature on WebDAV/HTTP logs: a client's DELETE to a resource is correctly rejected with 403 by --no-delete, then the same client issues a MOVE for the same source path that returns 201/204, deleting or clobbering the file the policy was meant to protect. Correlating the blocked DELETE with the successful MOVE on the same source+path within a short window isolates deliberate bypass probing from benign WebDAV traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit control-flow: DELETE returns 403 while MOVE on the same source path returns 201 (rename) or 204 (Overwrite:T RemoveAll). Same src+URL pairing of a blocked delete and a successful move is the CVE-2026-64863 fingerprint, not a generic WebDAV template. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://api.osv.dev/v1/vulns/GO-2026-4606 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64863
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV servers (SharePoint, Nextcloud, IIS WebDAV) where a client legitimately DELETEs then MOVEs unrelated files
  • WebDAV-aware clients (Windows Explorer redirector, Cyberduck, Cadaver) that retry a delete as a move-to-trash operation
  • Backup/sync agents that receive 403 on a locked resource then rename it
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) legitimately probing WebDAV verbs during an authorized scan
  • Web app that returns 403 for DELETE by policy but permits MOVE for renames as intended design
Suppression filter
// Scope to hosts you know run goshs (WebDAV file drop), e.g. filter DstHostname/dest to the artifact-server inventory, and require the DELETE and MOVE to share the SAME SrcIpAddr and Url before alerting.
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the destination host is a goshs instance (banner `goshs/vX`) started with `--no-delete`/`-w`; pull the full request pair for src IP + URL and check whether the MOVE 204 carried `Overwrite: T`. 2) CONTAIN: Stop/patch the goshs service (upgrade to v2.1.4+ where MOVE is delete-gated) or restrict the WebDAV port to trusted IPs; snapshot the served directory before further loss. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all MOVE 2xx from the same src IP across the served tree, check filesystem delete/rename events by the goshs process, and review other goshs advisories (CVE-2026-50138 read-only/upload-only bypass) on the same host.
let Window = 60s;
let Blocked = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "DELETE" and HttpStatusCode == "403"
| project BlockTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, Url, DstHostname;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "MOVE" and HttpStatusCode in ("201","204")
| join kind=inner Blocked on SrcIpAddr, Url, DstHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (BlockTime .. BlockTime + Window)
| project TimeGenerated, BlockTime, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval blocked_delete=if(http_method=="DELETE" AND status==403,1,0), move_ok=if(http_method=="MOVE" AND (status==201 OR status==204),1,0)
| stats sum(blocked_delete) as blocked_deletes sum(move_ok) as move_success values(status) as statuses values(http_method) as verbs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src url dest
| where blocked_deletes>0 AND move_success>0
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.http_method="DELETE" AND Web.status=403) OR (Web.http_method="MOVE" AND Web.status IN (201,204)) by Web.src Web.url Web.http_method Web.status Web.dest _time span=1s

| stats sum(blocked_delete) as blocked_deletes sum(move_ok) as move_success values(status) as statuses values(http_method) as verbs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src url dest
| where blocked_deletes>0 AND move_success>0

goshs process deletes or renames files despite --no-delete (CVE-2026-64863 impact) AIActions on Objectives High
Confirms real data loss from the WebDAV MOVE bypass by hunting file deletion/rename events whose initiating process is goshs while its command line carries --no-delete. Because --no-delete is supposed to make goshs never remove files, any FileDeleted/FileRenamed originated by that process under that flag is the bypass executing (rename removes the source; Overwrite:T triggers RemoveAll on the destination). Rationale: Pins to two article facts: the initiating binary is `goshs`, and its `--no-delete` command line is what the deletion is supposed to be impossible under — so goshs itself performing FileDeleted/FileRenamed is direct impact confirmation of the MOVE bypass rather than a generic file-deletion query. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://api.osv.dev/v1/vulns/GO-2026-4606
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • goshs run WITHOUT --no-delete where deletion/rename is expected behaviour (filter requires --no-delete so this is largely excluded)
  • Authorized red-team using goshs as a legitimate file-drop and cleaning up its own artifacts
  • Operator manually restarting goshs and clearing the served directory
  • A differently-named binary containing the substring 'goshs' in an unrelated toolchain
  • Antivirus quarantining a file inside the goshs-served path (initiating process would be the AV, not goshs)
Suppression filter
// Already tight: the --no-delete requirement excludes normal goshs deletion. To further reduce noise, restrict FolderPath/TargetFilePath to the goshs served directory (the value passed to `-d`).
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the goshs command line to confirm `--no-delete`/`-w`, and list the deleted/renamed file paths and their prior contents from backups or file-audit history. 2) CONTAIN: Kill the goshs process and upgrade to v2.1.4+ (MOVE now delete-gated); restore any destroyed artifacts from snapshot; restrict the WebDAV port. 3) HUNT: Correlate each deletion timestamp with the WebDAV MOVE 2xx access-log entry (UC1) to identify the source IP, then sweep for the same actor touching other goshs hosts or exploiting sibling goshs CVEs (CVE-2026-50138).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "goshs"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, PreviousFolderPath, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable goshs deployment: WebDAV file-server started with --no-delete (CVE-2026-64863 exposure) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces hosts running a goshs instance launched with the --no-delete protection flag (and WebDAV enabled), which on goshs <= v2.1.3 / <= v1.1.4 is silently bypassable via MOVE. This is a pre-exploitation exposure hunt so defenders can patch to v2.1.4+ or firewall the WebDAV port before the DELETE/MOVE bypass is abused. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact vulnerable invocation (`goshs -w --no-delete -d ...` / `--webdav --no-delete`) and affected versions (<= 2.1.3 / <= 1.1.4). Finds the exploitable configuration itself, giving defenders a patch-before-abuse window rather than waiting for the MOVE to fire. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64863
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration tests / red-team engagements legitimately standing up goshs for file transfer
  • Security lab / training environments running goshs intentionally
  • Instances already upgraded to v2.1.4+ where the flag combination is present but the bug is patched (validate version from banner)
  • Internal-only goshs on an isolated segment where the WebDAV port is unreachable by untrusted clients
  • A wrapper script or alias named 'goshs' unrelated to the file server
Suppression filter
// Reduce authorized-usage noise by excluding known pentest jump hosts: | where DeviceName !in~ ("redteam-01","pentest-lab-01")  — populate with your sanctioned goshs operator hosts.
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the goshs version (banner `goshs/vX.Y.Z` or package metadata) and whether the WebDAV port is exposed to untrusted networks. 2) CONTAIN: If <= v2.1.3 (or v1 <= 1.1.4), upgrade to v2.1.4+ where MOVE is gated by --no-delete, or firewall the WebDAV listener to trusted IPs only. 3) HUNT: For any exposed vulnerable host, pivot to UC1 (DELETE-403/MOVE-2xx web-log correlation) and UC2 (goshs file deletion) to determine whether the bypass was already exercised, and inventory other goshs hosts org-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--webdav","-w")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--webdav","-w")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs started with vulnerable empty-credential SFTP config (-sftp -b 'user:' no -fkf) CVE-2026-62325 AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact vulnerable invocation described in the advisory: goshs launched with -sftp and a -b basic-auth pair whose username OR password segment is empty and WITHOUT -fkf, which collapses gliderlabs/ssh into NoClientAuth=true (unauthenticated SFTP). This is the tell-tale on-disk configuration that exposes the CVE-2026-62325 / CVE-2026-40884 auth bypass. Rationale: Uses the advisory's literal vulnerable invocation (`-b 'admin:' -sftp` with no `-fkf`) — the empty-username/empty-password regex plus the absence of the `-fkf` public-key fix flag is the precise on-disk marker of the NoClientAuth bypass, so it is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagement standing up goshs as an intended file-transfer server
  • Developer testing goshs locally with a throwaway empty password on loopback
  • CTF or lab environment intentionally running the vulnerable config
  • Security researcher reproducing the CVE for validation
  • goshs used internally with -b for HTTP but the empty-cred regex catching an unusual but intended user:pass form
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh") and DeviceName has_any ("lab","test","ctf"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process is genuinely goshs (hash/path) and read the full command line — verify the -b value truly has an empty username or password and that -fkf is absent; check whether the SFTP port is bound to a public interface. 2) Contain: kill the goshs process and block the listener port at host firewall; if internet-facing, treat as exposed and rotate any data served from that directory. 3) Hunt: pivot on inbound connections to that host/port (UC 'goshs SFTP listener inbound connection') and file read/write by the goshs PID (UC 'goshs SFTP file I/O') to determine whether an unauthenticated session already occurred.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-sftp" and ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where FileName startswith "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+'?(:[^'\s:]+|[^'\s:]+:)'?(\s|$)"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "-sftp" and CommandLine has "-b"
| where CommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where NewProcessName has "goshs" or CommandLine has "goshs"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+'?(:[^'\s:]+|[^'\s:]+:)'?(\s|$)"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs -b basic-auth flag with empty username or password segment AIExploitation Medium
Complementary broad hunt for any goshs process whose -b flag carries an empty credential segment (`user:` empty password = CVE-2026-62325, or `:pass` empty username = CVE-2026-40884), regardless of flag ordering or whether -sftp is adjacent. Catches vulnerable instances the strict co-occurrence alert may miss. Rationale: Keys on the advisory's root cause — a `-b` value with an empty username (`:pass`) or empty password (`user:`) segment — without requiring `-sftp` adjacency, so it surfaces both CVE variants and unusual flag orderings; HasSftp/HasFixFlag are projected so an analyst can immediately judge exploitability. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • goshs run with -b for HTTP basic auth using an intentionally blank password in a trusted internal setting
  • Automated deployment scripts templating a -b value where the password variable is unexpectedly empty
  • Pentest tooling deployments
  • Config-management run that populates goshs with a placeholder credential
  • Analyst-run reproduction of the CVE
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the HasSftp / HasFixFlag columns — an empty-cred goshs WITH -sftp and WITHOUT -fkf is exploitable; empty-cred on HTTP-only goshs is lower risk but still weak auth. 2) Contain: stop the process if it is exposed beyond loopback and notify the asset owner to re-launch with a full user:password and -fkf. 3) Hunt: check the host's inbound connection and file telemetry for any session that landed during the exposure window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName startswith "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+'?(:[^'\s:]+|[^'\s:]+:)'?(\s|$)"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend HasSftp = tostring(ProcessCommandLine has "-sftp"), HasFixFlag = tostring(ProcessCommandLine has "-fkf")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, HasSftp, HasFixFlag, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "goshs" or CommandLine has "goshs"
| where CommandLine has "-b"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+'?(:[^'\s:]+|[^'\s:]+:)'?(\s|$)"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend HasSftp = tostring(CommandLine has "-sftp"), HasFixFlag = tostring(CommandLine has "-fkf")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, HasSftp, HasFixFlag
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs SFTP listener accepting inbound connections (post-bypass access) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces inbound network sessions accepted by the goshs process — the actual unauthenticated SFTP access enabled by the empty-credential bypass. Projects the remote IP and local port so the analyst sees whether the source is external and which (often non-standard, e.g. 2121) port the listener is bound to. Rationale: Pivots on the goshs process itself accepting inbound connections (advisory: 'SFTP accepts connections without password'), projecting RemoteIP/LocalPort rather than hardcoding a port, so a public source IP or the PoC's non-standard 2121 listener stands out as likely unauthenticated access. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm
ATT&CKT1133 T1021.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authorized SFTP transfers to an intentionally deployed goshs file server
  • Internal automation pulling files from a goshs instance
  • Vulnerability scanner probing the SFTP port
  • Pentest team's own client connecting during an engagement
  • Health-check / monitoring probe hitting the listener port
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RemoteIP — an external/public source connecting to a goshs SFTP listener that was launched with an empty credential (correlate with UC1 on the same host) is high concern. 2) Contain: firewall-block the source IP and the listener port; if the goshs config is confirmed vulnerable, terminate the process. 3) Hunt: enumerate files read/written by the goshs PID during the session (UC 'goshs SFTP file I/O') to scope data exposure and check for uploaded webshells/tooling.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "goshs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort
| summarize Sessions = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(LocalPort), Sources = make_set(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "goshs"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort
| summarize Sessions = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Ports = make_set(LocalPort), Sources = make_set(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc

goshs process file read/write/delete/rename via bypassed SFTP AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts filesystem operations performed by the goshs process, which serves file read/write/delete/rename over the unauthenticated SFTP channel. After a confirmed empty-credential bypass, a burst of file I/O by the goshs PID indicates data staging, exfiltration read, or attacker upload. Rationale: The advisory states the bypass yields 'read, write, delete, rename' file access; keying file operations on the goshs process as the initiating/context image ties filesystem I/O directly to the vulnerable service, and the distinct-file threshold suppresses idle-server noise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm
ATT&CKT1105 T1039
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized users legitimately transferring files through an intended goshs SFTP server
  • goshs used as a sanctioned internal file-drop with normal write volume
  • Backup or sync job reading files served by goshs
  • Pentest engagement staging tools through goshs
  • goshs serving a large directory tree where routine reads inflate the file count
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the file-op burst with an inbound session (UC 'goshs SFTP listener inbound') and the vulnerable-config alert (UC1) on the same host; review SampleFiles for sensitive paths or newly written executables/webshells. 2) Contain: stop the goshs process and quarantine any attacker-written files; preserve the served directory for forensics. 3) Hunt: if uploads are present, hash and sweep the estate for the same files; if reads target sensitive data, scope exfiltration and rotate exposed secrets.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "goshs"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| summarize FileOps = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(FolderPath), Actions = make_set(ActionType), SampleFiles = make_set(FolderPath, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctFiles >= 5
| order by FileOps desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| summarize FileOps = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(TargetFilePath), Actions = make_set(EventType), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctFiles >= 5
| order by FileOps desc

Endpoint traffic to cubepilot.org during 24 Jul 2026 DNS-hijack / AiTM window AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for any host that resolved or connected to cubepilot.org or its subdomains (portal, discuss/forum, docs) during the 24 July 2026 DNS-hijack window, when traffic was redirected to attacker infrastructure holding fraudulent TLS certs. Any credentials entered on those services may have been captured. Surfaces the resolved RemoteIP so an analyst can identify the attacker-controlled address. Rationale: Anchors on the exact victim domain (cubepilot.org and subdomains portal/discuss/docs confirmed on CubePilot's own security notice) bounded to the 24 Jul 2026 hijack window; make_set on RemoteIP/DnsResponseName surfaces the attacker-controlled resolution so no attacker IP needs to be hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1557 T1584.002 T1056.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer legitimately browsing docs.cubepilot.org or the forum during the window without entering credentials
  • DNS query that resolved to the legitimate host if it occurred outside the actual redirection minutes (control was regained the same day)
  • Automated firmware/version-check services polling cubepilot.org on a schedule
  • CI/CD or package tooling pulling from CubePilot repos
  • Security team already testing/validating the domain post-incident
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ResolvedIPs for each hit; any answer outside CubePilot's normal hosting ASN during 24 Jul is the attacker endpoint — pivot all hosts sharing that IP. 2) Contain: force password reset for any user who authenticated to portal/forum/docs on 24 Jul (creds may be captured) and revoke active sessions; block the attacker IP. 3) Hunt: search auth logs for the affected users signing in from anomalous IPs post-24 Jul, and check for password reuse alerts across SSO/VPN/email.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-07-24T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-07-26T00:00:00Z))
| where RemoteUrl has "cubepilot.org"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), ResolvedIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen asc
ImDnsActivity

| where DnsQuery has "cubepilot.org"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count(), ResolvedIPs=make_set(DnsResponseName, 25) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by FirstSeen asc

CubePilot firmware/file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 Jul 2026 (possible tampered supply chain) AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for firmware images or any file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 July 2026 — the window CubePilot flagged as unverified pending checksum review. Files pulled while attacker infrastructure served the domain may be trojanised; this surfaces the filenames and SHA256 so analysts can quarantine and compare against CubePilot's confirmed-good hashes before any flashing. Rationale: Keys on FileOriginUrl containing cubepilot.org bounded to the exact 24-25 Jul window CubePilot said needs checksum verification; projecting SHA256/FileName lets an analyst diff against confirmed-good firmware hashes. Datadog/Falcon left blank because Sysmon EID11 and FDR FileWritten do not carry the download-origin URL needed to tie a firmware file back to cubepilot.org. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1584.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Firmware download later confirmed clean once CubePilot publishes verified checksums
  • Documentation/PDF or non-firmware asset pulled from cubepilot.org (not a flashable image)
  • Re-download of a pre-24 Jul firmware that a developer already had
  • File served from a CDN/mirror rather than the hijacked origin
  • Automated build agent caching CubePilot artifacts
Suppression filter
| where FileName has_any (".apj",".px4",".bin",".hex",".elf")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list distinct SHA256 + FileName from the hits; compare each hash against CubePilot's confirmed-good firmware manifest — any hash not on the allow-list is suspect. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block flashing on affected engineering hosts, and isolate any UAV/bench system that was already flashed from a 24-25 Jul image pending inspection. 3) Hunt: on hosts that downloaded a suspect image, look for the flashing tool executing (ground-station/uploader), unexpected child processes, and outbound connections from the file's downloading process to non-CubePilot IPs.

| where FileOriginUrl has "cubepilot.org"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenAI models used Artifactory zero-days to escape to the internet

BleepingComputer
2026-07-28 6 use cases 1 technique 6 kill-chain phases detected

JFrog has confirmed that OpenAI models exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in self-hosted Artifactory servers to help escape an isolated testing environment and gain access to the internet before attacking Hugging Face. [...]

CVEsCVE-2026-65921 CVE-2026-65923 CVE-2026-65924 CVE-2026-65925 CVE-2026-66014 CVE-2026-66015 CVE-2026-65617 CVE-2026-66018
